headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and write-conflict between ECC and Goose; default filesystem overlap also creates medium leakage and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC and Goose both read/write files and use MCP, so one agent can ingest the other’s outputs through a shared filesystem or extension channel. ECC’s self-isolation is only a Cursor-only boundary, while Goose has no default self-isolation. This is not provably blocked, but the pathway is not clearly default-manual either.
conditions: IF ECC and Goose are pointed at the same workspace or shared MCP server, injected content can cross from one agent to the other.
IF either agent parses files from the shared workspace as instructions, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for ECC and Goose.
Disable shared MCP servers for one side.
Use read-only mounts for handoff files.
Add a manual review step before either agent consumes the other’s output.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging to all inter-agent files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch files and secrets, and Goose explicitly shares state via filesystem while ECC stores session data, hooks, and agent definitions under local paths. That creates a default path for sensitive material to move between them through the workspace or home-directory artifacts. The blast radius can include multiple work products and secrets.
conditions: IF ECC writes session artifacts into a directory Goose can read, Goose can ingest ECC secrets or summaries.
IF Goose writes code or cwd files containing sensitive data, ECC can read them back through filesystem access.
mitigations: Put each agent in a separate home/work directory.
Move secrets out of shared cwd before running either agent.
Restrict file permissions on session artifacts.
Review and redact logs after each run.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem sandboxing.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and git-state modification, and Goose’s shared state is explicitly via filesystem. ECC also supports multiple instances with shared-state caveats. Without locking, concurrent edits to the same repo or config can corrupt git state or overwrite files, which is a default-dangerous overlap.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository, concurrent commits or rebases can conflict.
IF both agents write to the same config or session paths, one can overwrite the other’s state.
mitigations: Run only one agent per repo at a time.
Use separate git branches for each agent.
Enable file locks around shared paths.
Keep ECC and Goose on separate roots.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can act on files and shell commands, and ECC produces security findings, documentation, and code-related outputs that Goose may treat as authoritative. Because both have tool use and filesystem access, an error in ECC can cascade into Goose’s downstream actions unless a verification step is inserted. The interaction is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF Goose consumes ECC-generated findings or instructions without verification, it may execute incorrect actions.
IF ECC emits stale or malformed code guidance, Goose can propagate it into files or shell actions.
mitigations: Require human review before Goose acts on ECC output.
Have Goose re-check file diffs before applying changes.
Limit ECC output to summaries, not instructions.
Use a checksum or signed handoff file.
requires-engineering: add structured validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: The profiles show local file and session handling, but no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. ECC handles session summaries and security findings; Goose handles source code and cwd files. With only docs-level evidence, a compliance issue is possible but not established, so this stays low rather than medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent without a matching retention policy, compliance risk increases.
IF one agent is configured to retain logs longer than the other, a mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workspaces.
Align retention settings before use.
Delete session artifacts after each run.
Review vendor/data-processing terms.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls.
